CHIEF COMPLAINT
Worsening headaches and newly diagnosed pituitary lesion

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
This is a 52-year-old male with a newly diagnosed pituitary lesion seen in neurology consultation at the request of Dr. Henry Howard for evaluation and possible surgical intervention. The patient initially presented to his primary care provider, Dr. Henry Howard, on 3/1/21 complaining of worsening headaches over the past few months with no prior history of headaches. Workup for the headaches with brain MRI and serology incidentally discovered a pituitary lesion. The patient describes his headaches as located behind his eyes with a dull, nagging quality. Onset was gradual approximately three months ago, initially 3/10 in severity and progressively worsening to current 6/10 severity. Headaches are worse in the morning and typically last a few hours with nothing that makes them better or worse. He denies radiation of pain. The patient reports recently bumping into door frames. He denies fever, rash, neck stiffness, numbness, tingling, or syncope. Vision was last checked in the fall with no changes noted at that time.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for fever, rash, neck stiffness, numbness, tingling, syncope, or balance changes. No other active complaints.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
No significant past medical history.

MEDICATIONS
No regular medications. Tried acetaminophen several times for headache relief without benefit.

ALLERGIES
Not documented

FAMILY HISTORY
Patient was adopted and has no knowledge of family medical history.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Works as a computer programmer. Married for 25 years and recently purchased a home. Denies alcohol, tobacco, and recreational drug use, never having used these substances.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Alert and oriented to time, place, and person. Appropriate affect, fluent speech.
Neurological: Cranial nerves grossly intact. No focal motor or sensory deficits in upper or lower extremities. Visual acuity normal. Eye movements normal. Pupils equal and reactive. Visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia. Color vision normal.

RESULTS
Laboratory (3/3/21): CBC, BMP, coagulation studies, and CRP all normal. Pituitary hormone profile with low TSH; all other results normal.
Imaging: MRI brain with contrast (3/4/21) shows well-defined pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of the optic chiasm. Ventricles normal in size. No other abnormalities noted.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Benign-appearing pituitary adenoma with optic chiasmal compression and bitemporal hemianopia. Surgical intervention indicated with transsphenoidal approach for excision and decompression. Risks of anesthesia (myocardial infarction, stroke, death) and surgery (infection, further surgery needed, cerebrospinal fluid leak, seizure, stroke, permanent neurological deficits, death) discussed with patient. Patient understands and consents to proceed. Referral to ophthalmology for comprehensive examination and visual field testing prior to surgery for baseline comparison. Pathology will be obtained from surgical specimen. Surgery to be scheduled expeditiously with surgical scheduler. Patient counseled regarding potential for vision improvement postoperatively without guarantees.
